title: Trump to Nominate Doctor Who Has Publicly Supported Vaccines as C.D.C. Director
summary:
President Trump has nominated Dr. Erica Schwartz, a physician and former deputy surgeon general, to serve as director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The selection of Dr. Schwartz, who has expressed support for vaccines while also emphasizing diet and exercise, marks a shift from Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s vaccine skepticism ahead of midterm elections. If confirmed by the Senate, she would become the agency’s fourth leader in just over a year and would oversee operations amid staff reductions, a headquarters shooting, and declining public trust.

Dr. Schwartz holds degrees in biomedical engineering, medicine, public health, and law, and previously managed federal drive-through coronavirus testing sites. Mr. Kennedy stated he looked forward to collaborating with her to restore trust and scientific integrity at the CDC. Public health experts have welcomed her credentials, while some of Mr. Kennedy’s allies have criticized her past enforcement of vaccine mandates.

The administration also named Sean Slovenski as deputy director and chief operating officer, Dr. Jennifer Shuford as deputy director and chief medical officer, and Dr. Sara Brenner as a senior counselor. The agency has operated without a permanent director for most of the current administration following earlier departures and acting leadership arrangements.

title: The contradiction at the heart of Republicans’ embrace of psychedelics
summary:
President Trump signed an executive order expanding access to psychedelics for mental health treatment, joined by podcaster Joe Rogan. Republican figures including Rick Perry, along with lawmakers such as Dan Crenshaw, Morgan Luttrell, and Jack Bergman, have promoted ibogaine and other substances like MDMA and psilocybin for treating veterans’ PTSD, traumatic brain injury, and addiction. Texas has allocated tens of millions for related research.

Clinicians with experience in addiction and psychiatric care note that psychedelics can interrupt withdrawal or ease symptoms but do not function in isolation. Sustained recovery from addiction, trauma, and serious mental illness depends primarily on social support and recovery capital, including stable housing, employment, healthcare access, and community connections. Research consistently identifies these factors as stronger predictors of long-term outcomes than pharmacological intervention alone.

The article observes that many advocates of psychedelic research have backed tax and spending measures reducing Medicaid, food assistance, and other programs that supply these resources. It states that such policies remove material conditions shown to support recovery, creating a gap between promoted treatments and the broader conditions required for their effectiveness.

title: Nebraska begins Medicaid work requirements ahead of federal deadline
summary: Nebraska’s Department of Health and Human Services began implementing new work requirements for certain Medicaid recipients on Friday, becoming the first state to adopt the policy ahead of a federal deadline. The requirements apply to adults covered under Medicaid expansion and are being phased in starting May 1, with full implementation scheduled through mid-2027. They originate from federal legislation known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill,” which directs states to enforce work rules for able-bodied adults ages 19 to 64 by January 1, 2027. Most expansion enrollees must complete at least 80 hours per month of qualifying activities such as employment, schooling, job training, or volunteering, or meet an equivalent income threshold. New applicants must comply immediately, while current enrollees will be assessed at their next eligibility renewal. Officials plan to verify compliance using existing data and have conducted outreach through mailed notices, texts, emails, and advertising. Exemptions apply to individuals with disabilities, pregnant people, and those facing temporary hardships. Nationally, analyses project that the policy could result in millions losing coverage by 2034, largely due to administrative hurdles, with the Congressional Budget Office estimating an overall increase of about 16 million uninsured individuals when combined with other changes. Most states intend to implement closer to the 2027 deadline.

title: RFK Jr. Wants to Wean Some Americans Off Antidepressants
summary:
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced measures to promote nondrug approaches, such as lifestyle changes, for treating depression and to assist patients in discontinuing psychiatric medications, including antidepressants. He stated that many patients start these drugs without adequate information on risks, duration of use, or withdrawal methods. The department plans to issue guidance encouraging alternatives to medication, while the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services will allow reimbursement for physicians monitoring tapering and outcomes. A federal panel will also develop protocols and training on medication risks and deprescribing for health centers. 

Kennedy emphasized that the initiatives aim to support informed decisions rather than mandate discontinuation. Antidepressants remain widely prescribed, with 16.6 percent of U.S. adults using them, though evidence shows limited benefits beyond placebo for many patients. Concerns have grown over prolonged withdrawal symptoms, prompting patient groups to seek stronger Food and Drug Administration warnings. Use has increased notably among younger women, amid social media promotion and debates over long-term effectiveness.

title: Food stamp work rules don't increase employment, researchers say
summary:
In Mingo County, West Virginia, residents waited several hours in a lengthy vehicle line for the House of Hope mobile food pantry. A delayed delivery from the Facing Hunger Foodbank postponed distribution of groceries including chicken, eggs, produce, and milk. Many recipients, such as Perry Hall, who receives Social Security for multiple myeloma, and his wife Lilly, rely on SNAP benefits alongside pantry assistance as monthly resources dwindle.

Federal changes under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act expanded work requirements to able-bodied adults aged 64 or younger without dependents, restricting benefits to three months every three years unless recipients work, volunteer, or train at least 80 hours monthly. The rules now cover parents of children 14 and older and eliminated exemptions for veterans, homeless individuals, and former foster youth. Similar expansions affect Kentucky.

Analysts note that prior requirements showed no measurable increase in employment or hours worked, with barriers including scarce jobs, transportation limits, and health issues cited as factors. States will assume higher SNAP administrative costs beginning in October. Local pantries operated by volunteers continue distributions, while some recipients secure limited employment to maintain eligibility.

title: Why Congress failed to reach an Obamacare deal
summary: Congressional efforts to extend enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies ended without agreement after months of stalled negotiations. A bipartisan House group led by Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick introduced a one-year extension measure in September, citing warnings that expiration would sharply raise premiums for millions of enrollees. The Congressional Budget Office projected nearly four million people would lose coverage over the decade, while polls showed broad public support for continuation. Talks repeatedly broke down over the Hyde amendment limiting federal abortion funding, Republican concerns about fraud on the exchanges, and the estimated $350 billion cost. The issue became linked to government funding deadlines, contributing to a 43-day shutdown. Senate negotiations produced no compromise, and the White House offered limited direction. Subsidies expired at the end of 2025, producing premium increases and lower enrollment for 2026. Both parties attributed the outcome to the other’s positions.

title: Federal judge halts RFK Jr.'s changes to children's vaccine policies
summary: A federal judge in Boston has blocked key elements of the Trump administration’s efforts to revise national vaccine policies. U.S. District Court Judge Brian Murphy ruled Monday that Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. improperly replaced all members of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices. The decision stays the appointments of 13 new members installed since June 2025 and forces postponement of a committee meeting scheduled for later in the week. The ruling responded to a lawsuit brought by the American Academy of Pediatrics and other health organizations, which argued that the changes bypassed established scientific procedures. Judge Murphy determined that the administration’s actions were arbitrary and capricious and undermined the integrity of vaccine policy development. The committee had been expected to examine COVID-19 vaccines and consider revisions to recommendations such as hepatitis B vaccination for newborns. The Department of Health and Human Services said it will appeal, while the plaintiffs called the outcome a victory for evidence-based public health.

title: Seniors Paid Billions in Extra Premiums Due to Alleged Medicare Overpayments
summary:
A congressional committee reported that overpayments to private Medicare Advantage plans raised Medicare Part B premiums by an average of $212 per year, or about 10%, for seniors in 2025. The Joint Economic Committee attributed the $13.4 billion increase to billing practices by insurers, including the addition of diagnoses that trigger higher payments. Both beneficiaries in Medicare Advantage and traditional Medicare faced these higher costs, which are deducted from Social Security checks.

The report, prepared by the committee’s Republican staff and released Tuesday, drew on estimates from the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission indicating that Medicare Advantage costs approximately 20% more than traditional Medicare for similar enrollees. Major insurers such as UnitedHealth Group, Humana, and Elevance Health participate in the program.

The health insurance industry group AHIP criticized the findings as relying on flawed data and methodology. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services declined to comment on the external analysis. Medicare agency administrator Mehmet Oz stated that while payment incentives have sometimes been misaligned, insurers may not be overpaid to the extent suggested. Recent regulatory changes aim to limit certain practices used to increase reimbursements.

title: FDA backs away from RFK Jr.’s claims about drug’s promise for autism patients
summary:
The Food and Drug Administration has determined that it lacks sufficient evidence to support the use of leucovorin for treating autism. This position differs from statements made in September by FDA Commissioner Marty Makary, who described the drug as a promising therapy that could help hundreds of thousands of children with autism and cited studies showing improvements in verbal communication among those with folate deficiency.

On Tuesday, the agency approved leucovorin for FOLR1-related cerebral folate transport deficiency, an ultra-rare genetic disease affecting fewer than one in a million people. The approval applies to children and adults and notes that the treatment may benefit some patients who experience developmental delays with autistic features. Officials said the data met evidentiary standards for this specific condition but not for autism more broadly.

A randomized controlled trial previously referenced in support of autism use was retracted earlier this year due to errors. The FDA relied on a systematic literature review rather than new trials for the rare-disease approval. Senior officials stated that the agency is open to additional studies on leucovorin for autism and that patients may discuss off-label use with physicians, while confirming the drug is not currently in shortage.

title: Federal court blocks Kennedy’s vaccine changes, invalidates vaccine advisory panel
summary: A federal judge has blocked changes to U.S. vaccine policy implemented by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., including alterations to the recommended childhood immunization schedule and the reconstitution of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP). U.S. District Judge Brian E. Murphy granted a preliminary injunction sought by the American Academy of Pediatrics, ruling that the remaking of the ACIP last year violated the Federal Advisory Committee Act. The decision invalidates all votes taken by the committee since its reconstitution. Murphy also determined that the CDC’s decision to bypass the ACIP when revising the childhood immunization schedule was arbitrary and capricious, as it departed from longstanding practice without adequate explanation. The ruling noted that many newly appointed ACIP members lacked sufficient expertise in vaccines or immunizations, despite possessing qualifications in other areas. The changes implemented by the new committee included ending routine birth doses of the hepatitis B vaccine, delaying the combined measles, mumps, rubella, and varicella vaccine, and shifting COVID-19 vaccine recommendations. The Department of Health and Human Services stated it would appeal the decision. The order effectively prevents the current ACIP members from serving but does not block upcoming meetings outright.

title: Anti-Abortion March Brings Thousands to D.C., and a Sense of Frustration
summary: At the annual March for Life rally in Washington, Vice President JD Vance addressed anti-abortion activists’ concerns that the Trump administration has not moved quickly enough to restrict abortion access. Although the movement credits President Trump’s first-term judicial appointments with the Supreme Court’s reversal of Roe v. Wade, participants expressed frustration over the Food and Drug Administration’s approval of a generic abortion pill and Trump’s suggestion that Republicans show flexibility on the Hyde Amendment. Vance acknowledged these worries, pledged continued progress over the next three years, and framed the issue in moral terms. The administration announced several measures, including reinstatement of a ban on federal funding for research using human fetal tissue, expansion of restrictions on international organizations that perform or promote abortions, and an investigation into Planned Parenthood’s pandemic-era loans. Activists pressed for stronger steps, such as enforcement of the Comstock Act to limit mailing of abortion pills. Some state-level restrictions have advanced more rapidly than federal policy. Reproductive rights groups warned that these efforts could affect access nationwide. Pope Leo XIV sent a supportive message to participants.

title: Supreme Court restores abortion pill access — for now
summary: Justice Samuel Alito issued a brief order Monday temporarily staying a ruling by the 5th Circuit Court of Appeals that had restricted access to the abortion drug mifepristone. The order restores, through May 11, the prior availability of the medication via telehealth prescriptions and mail delivery in states where abortion remains legal. Alito’s action provides time for the full Supreme Court to consider emergency requests from manufacturers Danco and GenBioPro, which argued that the appeals court decision would create regulatory uncertainty for drug sponsors, providers, and patients. Louisiana was directed to file a response by May 7. Some telehealth abortion providers suspended services or shifted to misoprostol-only regimens after the 5th Circuit ruling, prompting questions from patients about previously obtained doses. Planned Parenthood and other advocacy groups described heightened confusion among patients and providers. Anti-abortion organizations criticized the stay and called for broader federal limits on the medication. The drug is used in more than two-thirds of U.S. abortions.

title: RFK Jr. launches plan to address ‘overuse’ of psychiatric medications
summary: US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced a federal plan to reduce overprescribing of psychiatric medications, promote alternative treatments, and support discontinuation when appropriate. The announcement, made at a MAHA Institute summit, emphasized addressing the nation’s mental health crisis, especially among children, through greater patient autonomy, informed consent, shared decision-making, and a shift toward prevention and holistic care. The effort follows recent guidelines from the American Society of Clinical Psychopharmacology on appropriate discontinuation practices. Some psychiatry experts welcomed increased attention to these issues but raised concerns about an overemphasis on overprescribing at a time when access to mental health care remains limited. Kennedy has previously cited risks associated with the medications, including links to violence, fetal harm, severe withdrawal, and effects on children. The US Food and Drug Administration has deemed the drugs generally safe and effective for disorders such as depression, anxiety, and obsessive-compulsive disorder. Experts noted that both overprescribing and underprescribing can occur and that decisions should weigh individual benefits against potential harms.

title: Fertility treatment given special emphasis as Trump Rx site goes live
summary: TrumpRx, a federal drug discount program, launched earlier this month offering coupons for 43 medications, four of which are used in IVF procedures. Experts described the initiative as a partial step toward fulfilling a 2024 campaign pledge to expand IVF access. The platform provides discounts mainly on fertility drugs, GLP-1 agonists, and menopause medications, though pharmaceutical costs represent only 10 to 20 percent of total IVF expenses. Federal estimates project savings of up to $2,200 per cycle, while a full cycle can reach $30,000 out of pocket. The Heritage Foundation, which has shaped aspects of current policy, has opposed IVF on the grounds that embryos constitute human life and has promoted alternatives such as intrauterine insemination when limited to married couples. Specialists in reproductive medicine noted that these positions create tension between certain ethical frameworks and clinical practice, while the administration indicated that further discounts may be added in coming months.

title: Trump urges GOP to be ‘flexible’ on Hyde Amendment, igniting backlash from pro-life allies
summary: Pro-life organizations have criticized President Donald Trump’s remarks urging Republican lawmakers to show flexibility on the Hyde Amendment, a 1976 provision that bars most federal funding for abortions. The comments came during a House Republican policy retreat focused on healthcare legislation, including efforts to revive expired Obamacare subsidies while imposing new limits on abortion coverage. Groups including Students for Life Action and SBA Pro-Life America stated that Republicans should reject any compromise on taxpayer-funded abortions and called for upholding the amendment without exception. Several conservative commentators and lawmakers expressed similar opposition, describing the amendment as a longstanding party principle. One Republican senator said he was not flexible on the value of every child’s life. Trump had previously issued an executive order reinforcing the Hyde Amendment early in his current term. The remarks occurred as Republicans prepare for midterm elections and continue internal debates over healthcare policy.

title: Exclusive: U.S. and Iran closing in on one-page memo to end war, officials say
summary: The White House is reportedly close to reaching an agreement with Iran on a one-page memorandum of understanding to end the war and outline a framework for subsequent nuclear negotiations. U.S. officials and other sources indicate that Iranian responses on several key points are expected within the next 48 hours, representing the nearest the parties have come to a deal since the conflict began. The memorandum would include Iran committing to a moratorium on nuclear enrichment, the United States agreeing to lift sanctions and release billions in frozen Iranian funds, and both sides easing restrictions on transit through the Strait of Hormuz. Many provisions would depend on a final agreement. The document is being negotiated by U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner with Iranian officials, directly and through mediators. It would declare an end to the war and initiate a 30-day period of talks on detailed terms, potentially in Islamabad or Geneva. The length of the enrichment moratorium is under negotiation, with proposals ranging from 12 to 15 years. Iran would also commit to forgoing nuclear weapons, accepting enhanced inspections, and possibly removing highly enriched uranium. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio described the issues as complex and technical while noting uncertainty about Iranian leaders’ readiness to conclude an accord.

title: What We Know About the Memo the U.S. and Iran Are Discussing
summary: The U.S. and Iran, working through mediators, are developing a one-page, 14-point memorandum of understanding to outline a month of negotiations aimed at ending hostilities. The document proposes that talks could begin as early as next week in Islamabad, Pakistan. Iran has indicated willingness to address its nuclear program, while the draft calls for easing restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for the U.S. reducing its blockade of Iranian ports during the 30-day period. Discussions also include the possible transfer of some Iranian highly enriched uranium stockpiles to third countries, though Iran has rejected any direct handover to the United States. Unresolved issues include the duration of any enrichment suspension, Iran’s role in overseeing the strait, and the scope of sanctions relief. The one-month timeframe could be extended by mutual consent if progress occurs. Iran is currently reviewing the proposal, and multiple draft documents have circulated among the involved capitals. President Trump stated that the U.S. would resume military action if no agreement is reached.

title: Trump opens Hormuz under fire with ‘Project Freedom’ as Iran warns of attacks
summary: The U.S. military has initiated an operation called Project Freedom to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping. The effort involves guided-missile destroyers, more than 100 aircraft, unmanned systems, and roughly 15,000 service members, who are providing a layered defensive umbrella rather than individual escorts. U.S. Central Command reported that forces intercepted Iranian cruise missiles, drones, and small boats, destroying six attack vessels, and that two U.S.-flagged merchant ships completed transits without incident. Iranian officials rejected the claims of successful passages as baseless and stated that foreign forces entering the strait would be attacked. President Donald Trump warned that any Iranian strikes on U.S. vessels would face overwhelming retaliation. The waterway, which carries approximately one-quarter of the world’s seaborne oil trade, remains contested. Observers have noted limited independent confirmation of resumed large-scale traffic and raised questions about whether naval mines have been fully cleared. Additional vessels are expected to attempt passage as the operation continues.

title: UAE to leave OPEC amid Hormuz oil crisis, a blow to Saudi Arabia
summary:
The United Arab Emirates announced Tuesday that it would withdraw from the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and the wider OPEC+ alliance, effective May 1. The decision follows years of reported tensions with Saudi Arabia over production quotas and comes as the Iran war and related closures of the Strait of Hormuz create global energy supply disruptions. UAE Energy Minister Suhail Al Mazrouei cited the country’s long-term strategic vision and changing energy profile as reasons for the exit, while thanking OPEC members for decades of cooperation.

A founding participant through Abu Dhabi in 1967 and a full member since 1971, the UAE ranks as OPEC’s third-largest producer. Its departure leaves eleven core members and follows Qatar’s exit in 2019. Analysts noted that the move reflects the UAE’s economic diversification into trade, tourism, transportation, and emerging sectors such as artificial intelligence, which has reduced its reliance on high oil prices compared with some neighbors. Observers also pointed to recent strains in Saudi-UAE relations stemming from events in Yemen. Because the Strait of Hormuz remains largely closed, the immediate effect on global oil output and prices is expected to be limited.

title: Trump Tells Aides to Prepare for Extended Blockade of Iran
summary: President Trump has instructed aides to prepare for an extended naval blockade of Iran, seeking to pressure the regime into dismantling its nuclear program by restricting oil exports and access to ports. Following an April cease-fire, Trump reviewed options that included resuming airstrikes or withdrawing U.S. forces and concluded that maintaining the blockade posed fewer immediate risks than the alternatives. The measure has reduced tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, raised global fuel prices, and contributed to lower presidential approval ratings ahead of midterm elections. Iran’s recent proposal to reopen the strait while postponing nuclear talks was rejected as insufficient. Although the blockade has limited Iranian oil sales and prompted new contacts with Washington, it leaves U.S. forces committed to the region without a clear timetable for Iranian concessions. Administration officials report divided counsel, with some favoring sustained economic pressure and others warning of broader economic damage. Talks remain stalled while Iranian leaders consult internally, and observers note that both governments appear to believe time works in their favor.

title: Trump calls Iran’s proposal ‘totally unacceptable’
summary: President Trump expressed strong disapproval of Iran’s reply to his administration’s peace proposal, stating on Truth Social that he found the response “totally unacceptable.” Iranian state media confirmed that negotiators in Tehran had delivered their answer earlier the same day. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and senior officials have served as intermediaries in the discussions between Washington and Tehran. The U.S. proposal reportedly called for Iran to halt uranium enrichment in return for sanctions relief and eased restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. According to multiple reports, Iran’s counteroffer instead prioritizes an immediate end to fighting and a gradual reopening of the strait while deferring detailed nuclear arrangements for further talks within a 30-day period. Tehran suggested diluting some enriched uranium and moving the remainder to a third country, with provisions for its return if talks collapse. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi stated that the country would not submit to pressure and that its armed forces remained fully prepared to defend national interests.

title: Senate Republicans again reject resolution to rein in Trump's Iran war
summary: The Republican-led Senate voted 47-52 on Wednesday to reject a Democratic resolution that would have required the withdrawal of U.S. forces from the conflict with Iran unless Congress authorized further military action. The vote was the fourth this year in which the Senate declined to reclaim its war powers. Under the War Powers Act of 1973, Congress must authorize the use of force within 60 days of the conflict’s start, a deadline that falls at the end of the month, with a possible 30-day extension. Several Republican senators, including Lisa Murkowski and Susan Collins, have discussed drafting an authorization measure or requiring a vote if the conflict continues, while others have called for a clear plan to conclude operations. Senate Majority Leader John Thune noted that a future request for war funding could give Congress leverage. Democratic senators described the war as illegal and unnecessary, arguing that continued Republican support prevents oversight and prolongs an unjustified conflict. The result of an expected House vote on similar measures remains uncertain.

title: What has the U.S. war with Iran accomplished?
summary: President Trump's stated aims in the conflict with Iran included ending its nuclear program, destroying its military capabilities, and achieving regime change. After more than five weeks of fighting and a two-week ceasefire, these objectives remain unmet. Iran's military suffered extensive damage to its navy, air force, and missile and drone programs, according to U.S. officials, yet it continues to function and conduct strikes across the region. Iran retains control of the Strait of Hormuz, imposing restrictions and fees on shipping that have raised global oil prices, a development that arose during the war. The ceasefire has largely held, though conflicting reports have emerged regarding attacks on infrastructure and strait access. Iran's nuclear program persists, and the conflict, along with the death of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, may have reinforced hard-line leadership under his son Mojtaba, potentially increasing Tehran's interest in nuclear weapons. The U.S. decision not to warn Gulf allies contributed to regional strikes and economic disruptions, eroding confidence among partners.

title: Advocates of a two-state solution realise time to act is now
summary:
British Prime Minister Keir Starmer stated that the UK would recognise a Palestinian state at the UN General Assembly in September if Israel failed to meet certain conditions. The announcement coincided with efforts by several governments to advance a two-state solution amid reports that Israeli officials are pursuing settlement expansion in Gaza and de facto sovereignty in the West Bank.

A conference in New York, co-chaired by France and Saudi Arabia, produced the New York Declaration, which proposes a transitional administrative committee to govern Gaza under the Palestinian Authority following a ceasefire. The document calls for Hamas to end its rule and transfer weapons to the Authority, supports a possible UN-mandated international stabilisation mission, and stresses that Gaza must remain part of a unified Palestinian state alongside the West Bank. The Palestinian Authority indicated it would hold presidential elections within a year.

Israeli officials rejected the British conditions, making recognition by the UK appear likely in September. The declaration reflects attempts by European and Arab states to outline a postwar political framework while international patience with current Israeli policies appears to be diminishing.

title: Biden's Warning Over Rafah Sharpens a Problem for Netanyahu
summary: President Biden's warning that the United States may withhold additional weapons, including heavy bombs and artillery shells, has placed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu under increased pressure as he weighs international calls for a cease-fire against domestic demands for a large-scale operation in Rafah. Netanyahu stated that Israel would stand alone if necessary and proceed with its objectives. Israeli officials, including Defense Minister Yoav Gallant and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, asserted that the war effort against Hamas would continue regardless of U.S. restrictions. The Israeli military indicated it possesses sufficient munitions for planned operations in Rafah, though analysts noted that limits on specific U.S.-supplied weapons could require adjustments in targeting methods. The United States has already withheld 3,500 bombs intended for potential use in the area and is reviewing further transfers. Israeli diplomats described the decision as disappointing and argued it could embolden Hamas. The developments occur amid a Gaza death toll exceeding 34,000, according to local health authorities, and follow Israel's recent advance to the Rafah border crossing with Egypt.

title: U.S., Arab nations plan for postwar Gaza, timeline for Palestinian state
summary: The Biden administration and several Middle East partners are developing a detailed plan for long-term peace between Israel and the Palestinians that includes a timeline for establishing a Palestinian state. The effort is linked to negotiations for an initial cease-fire in Gaza and the release of hostages held by Hamas, which could begin before Ramadan starts on March 10. A pause in fighting of at least six weeks is intended to allow time for the plan to be announced, additional support secured, and steps taken such as forming an interim Palestinian government. Participants include Egypt, Jordan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Palestinian representatives, and the United States. U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken has described the goal as a practical, time-bound path to a Palestinian state living alongside Israel. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has expressed opposition to a Palestinian state and insisted on maintaining overriding security control west of the Jordan River. Concerns have been raised that an Israeli operation in Rafah could disrupt both the hostage talks and broader peace efforts. Some Arab officials have expressed optimism about creating a technocratic Palestinian government focused on security, economic revitalization, and Gaza reconstruction, with possible inclusion of Hamas political representatives. Skeptics have questioned whether current Israeli and Palestinian leadership would support such changes and whether the United States would extend early recognition of a Palestinian state.

title: Trump, Iran are locked in high-stakes standoff as oil prices hit 4-year high
summary: The United States and Iran remain locked in a standoff over the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and restrictions on Iran’s nuclear program. The U.S. blockade, supported by Iranian mines and drones, has stopped commercial shipping through the waterway, pushing Brent crude oil prices to $126 per barrel and the average U.S. gasoline price to $4.30 per gallon. President Trump has said the blockade will continue until Iran accepts limits that prevent it from acquiring nuclear weapons and has rejected proposals to address shipping access before nuclear issues. Iranian officials have offered to negotiate the reopening of the strait first, describing the restrictions as a temporary response to prior attacks, while signaling that military and hard-line factions oppose renewed concessions on uranium enrichment. Tehran maintains it can withstand economic pressure through established sanctions-evasion methods. International backing for U.S. efforts has not materialized, and talks remain suspended. Reports indicate increased arrests and executions inside Iran amid the economic strain, while both governments continue to advance maximalist positions.

title: The U.S.-backed Gaza aid plan has started operating. Why are so many humanitarian groups opposed to it?
summary:
The Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, a U.S.-backed organization approved by Israel, has begun operations to distribute aid in Gaza through a limited number of guarded hubs, despite opposition from the United Nations and most humanitarian groups. The group moved food supplies to four initial sites on Monday and said distribution had started, with plans to reach more than one million people by the end of the week. The hubs are located near Israeli military positions, primarily in the south. 

Jake Wood, the foundation’s American executive director, resigned days earlier, stating the organization would not be permitted to operate independently. The new system replaces the U.N.-led distribution network that has operated since October 2023. Israel has accused Hamas of diverting aid, while the United Nations and aid agencies deny significant losses and reject the mechanism, arguing it violates humanitarian principles and risks enabling forced displacement. 

GHF is led by American security contractors and former military personnel. Its funding sources remain unclear, and its long-term leadership is uncertain following Wood’s departure. The Hamas-run Interior Ministry has warned residents against cooperating with the foundation.

title: Gaza talks turn to key sticking points between Israel, Hamas
summary:
Delegations from Israel and Hamas began indirect negotiations in Egypt on Monday over U.S. President Donald Trump’s plan to end the war in Gaza. The talks, held at the Red Sea resort of Sharm El Sheikh with Egyptian, American, and Qatari intermediaries, addressed contentious issues including an Israeli withdrawal and Hamas disarmament. Both sides have endorsed the plan’s core principles, which call for a ceasefire, the release of hostages, and increased humanitarian aid, with support from several Arab and Western governments.

Hamas outlined positions on hostage releases and the timeline for an Israeli pullout while expressing concerns about guarantees for a permanent ceasefire. Israel indicated it would initially focus on hostage returns and limit any withdrawal to a designated buffer zone. Israeli strikes continued during the talks, with Gaza health authorities reporting 19 deaths in the preceding 24 hours.

The negotiations opened on the eve of the second anniversary of the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack, which killed 1,200 people and resulted in 251 hostages. Israel’s subsequent campaign has killed more than 67,000 Palestinians. Further sessions were scheduled for Tuesday, with U.S. officials noting that discussions would cover lists of hostages and prisoners for potential release.

title: What is Hamas and why is it fighting with Israel in Gaza?
summary:
Hamas is an armed Palestinian group and political movement that has governed the Gaza Strip since 2007. Founded in 1987 as an offshoot of the Muslim Brotherhood, it opposes Israel’s existence and seeks an Islamic state across historic Palestine, though it has indicated willingness to accept an interim state limited to the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and Gaza.

On 7 October 2023, Hamas launched an attack on Israel that killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. The assault prompted a major Israeli military offensive in Gaza, which has resulted in tens of thousands of Palestinian deaths. Hamas leaders Ismail Haniyeh and Yahya Sinwar were both killed in 2024, after which the group has been directed by a five-member council based primarily in Qatar and Turkey.

In October 2025, the first phase of a US-brokered ceasefire led to the release of the remaining living Israeli hostages and nearly 2,000 Palestinian prisoners. The agreement followed earlier rounds of conflict between the two sides and came amid international recognition of a Palestinian state by several countries.

title: Justices seem inclined to revive Trump policy blocking migrants at border
summary: The Supreme Court on Tuesday appeared inclined to allow the Trump administration to reinstate a policy known as metering, which permits border agents to turn away migrants seeking asylum before they reach U.S. soil. Lower courts had blocked the policy, ruling that immigration law requires officials to process asylum claims from individuals attempting to enter the country. The administration argues that only those physically inside the United States are entitled to apply for asylum under the relevant statutes. During oral arguments, several conservative justices questioned whether migrants stopped on the Mexican side of the border could be considered to have “arrived in” the United States. The policy originated on a limited basis during the Obama administration and was expanded under President Trump to manage surges at the border. Critics contend that it creates unsafe conditions in Mexico and may encourage illegal crossings. The Biden administration had rescinded the practice, but the current administration indicated it might revive metering if border conditions warrant. The case is one of several immigration matters before the Court.

title: Supreme Court considers letting Trump administration revive restrictive immigration asylum policy
summary: The Supreme Court on Tuesday considered whether the Trump administration could reinstate a metering policy that restricted the number of migrants permitted to apply for asylum at the U.S.-Mexico border. The policy, implemented to manage increased arrivals, was struck down by lower courts. Although not currently in effect, the administration maintains that metering serves as an essential tool available to previous administrations and should remain an option. During arguments, some conservative justices appeared open to the government's position, while others questioned whether the approach would favor individuals who entered the country unlawfully over those seeking entry at ports. The central legal dispute involves the interpretation of the phrase "arrive in" under the Immigration and Nationality Act, with the Justice Department arguing it applies only to those already inside the United States. Immigration advocates contend the law requires officials to allow asylum claims from anyone presenting at a port of entry. The metering practice originated during the Obama administration and was expanded under President Trump's first term before being discontinued amid the coronavirus pandemic. A district court and the Ninth Circuit ruled that the policy violated federal law and migrants' rights. The case is among several immigration matters before the court this term.

title: Trump administration separates thousands of migrant families in the US
summary:
During his first term, President Donald Trump’s zero-tolerance policy separated more than 5,000 children from their families at the U.S.-Mexico border. With illegal crossings now at their lowest levels in decades, enforcement has shifted inward, producing separations among mixed-status families already living in the United States. Federal authorities and local partners are detaining record numbers of migrants, averaging more than 66,000 people in November, the highest figure on record. Detainees are frequently transferred between facilities, held for weeks or months, and then deported or released under supervision.

Three families described recent separations. Antonio Laverde, who entered illegally in 2022 and later received work authorization, was arrested at his Miami home in June and deported to Venezuela after three months in detention. His wife and two young children, who hold refugee status, remain in Florida. In Miami, Yaoska’s husband was detained during an August immigration appointment, failed a credible-fear interview, and was deported to Nicaragua after three months at the Krome facility; she is pregnant and subject to electronic monitoring. Edgar, a long-term resident of South Florida, was detained by local police on an old traffic warrant, transferred to immigration custody, and deported to Guatemala in June, leaving his wife to support two children through informal work. Families report ongoing emotional and financial strain.

title: Democrats divided over Biden’s immigration executive order
summary: President Biden’s executive order restricting migrant access to the U.S. asylum system when daily illegal crossings exceed 2,500 has drawn sharp criticism from numerous congressional Democrats. The measure, announced Tuesday, follows repeated failures by Congress to pass legislation addressing border security, including a bipartisan bill that would have paired an asylum limit with additional enforcement funding. Republicans rejected the legislation after opposition from former President Trump. Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer acknowledged the executive action as preferable to inaction but noted legislation would be better. Biden stated he was acting because Republicans refused to do so. While some Democrats viewed the order as an attempt to appeal to independent voters, others argued it conceded to Republican demands, risked alienating the party base, and undermined asylum protections. Republicans described the move as too little, too late. Immigration ranks among voters’ top concerns ahead of the election, with polls showing Trump favored over Biden on the issue. Democratic lawmakers expressed differing views on whether the order went far enough or was overly restrictive, with most agreeing congressional action remains necessary.

title: US appeals court lets Texas keep river barrier against border crossings
summary: A U.S. appeals court has ruled that Texas can retain a 1,000-foot floating barrier of large buoys in the Rio Grande to deter illegal migrant crossings. The full 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals reversed a lower court’s preliminary injunction that had ordered the state to move the barrier from a shallow section of the river. The decision allows the structure to remain in place while the Biden administration’s lawsuit proceeds. That suit accuses Texas of violating federal environmental law by installing an obstruction in navigable waters without required approvals. A trial is scheduled to begin next week. The appeals court found that the district court had erred in determining the barrier was located in a navigable stretch of the river. The ruling supports Texas Governor Greg Abbott and Attorney General Ken Paxton in their Operation Lone Star initiative. The barrier is one of several state measures facing federal challenges over immigration authority.

title: US border security: What could Biden, Congress and Texas do?
summary: U.S. President Joe Biden is assessing whether he holds legal authority to restrict migrant entries at the U.S.-Mexico border after Republicans declined to advance bipartisan legislation that would grant such powers. In a recent interview, Biden indicated that immigration ranks among voters’ top concerns ahead of the November elections. Republicans have urged restoration of restrictive policies from the prior administration, including the “remain in Mexico” program and expanded border wall construction, while criticizing a Senate bill that would tighten asylum standards. The Republican-led state of Texas has enacted its own measure allowing state authorities to arrest and detain people suspected of unlawful presence, though federal courts have blocked its implementation. Under the U.S. system, Congress enacts immigration statutes and the executive branch enforces them, yet both branches have faced judicial challenges to their actions. Biden has requested additional funding for border personnel and supported emergency authority to return migrants when daily encounters reach certain thresholds. His administration is now examining possible unilateral steps, such as invoking existing statutes previously used to limit entries.

title: On US-Mexico bridge, two sides of Biden border crackdown
summary:
A group of mainly Venezuelan migrants deported from the United States under the Biden administration’s June 5 asylum restrictions walked back into Mexico across the El Paso-Ciudad Juarez bridge on Saturday. The men had crossed the border days earlier amid extreme heat and encountered other migrants waiting in line for interviews through the CBP One mobile app. Several deportees said they planned to attempt another crossing despite facing at least a five-year entry ban.

U.S. border apprehensions have fallen sharply since the policy took effect, reaching their lowest daily level since February 2021. At the same time, migrant shelters in Ciudad Juarez have recorded a nearly 40 percent rise in arrivals. One Salvadoran migrant died of dehydration near the city, and deaths in the El Paso sector have nearly doubled this fiscal year as rescues have tripled.

Migrants at shelters described the CBP One app as their only remaining legal pathway. A Venezuelan family whose infant was hospitalized after exposure to pepper balls fired by Texas National Guard troops said they were now waiting for an app appointment rather than risk another desert crossing. U.S. officials reported that most recent arrivals were not claiming fear of return and attributed many journeys to economic motives.

title: Where Trump and Harris stand on immigration and border security
summary: Immigration has become a central issue in the November election, with voters expressing concern over migrant numbers during the Biden administration. Republicans have criticized President Biden and Vice President Harris for an overwhelmed system that they say allows terrorists and criminals to enter the country. The administration initially promised a more humane approach but later imposed asylum restrictions while creating new legal pathways for migrants. Encounters at the southern border have declined this summer. As the Democratic nominee, Harris visited the border and proposed further limits on asylum claims, stressing enforcement and drug interdiction based on her prior experience as California attorney general. She has credited administration policies for the drop in crossings and supported a failed bipartisan bill to increase border resources. Harris advocates comprehensive reform that includes pathways to citizenship. Former President Trump has made immigration a focus of his campaign, promising the largest domestic deportation operation in U.S. history. He has said he would use the National Guard, invoke the Alien Enemies Act, reinstate the Remain in Mexico program and Title 42, expand travel bans, and end birthright citizenship for children of undocumented parents.

title: Harris promises tougher immigration, fentanyl controls at border
summary:
Vice President Kamala Harris visited the U.S.-Mexico border in Douglas, Arizona, on Friday during her presidential campaign. She called for tighter asylum restrictions, including barring re-entry for five years for those crossing illegally and denying asylum claims made outside legal ports of entry. Harris also pledged to make stopping fentanyl a top priority, revive a failed bipartisan border bill, and expand funding to prosecute cartels while targeting precursor chemicals from China. She emphasized creating a humane system that includes a citizenship pathway for Dreamers and rejected framing border security and orderly immigration as incompatible goals.

Harris accused Republican rival Donald Trump of blocking the border legislation and spreading division. Trump countered that Harris bears responsibility for record migrant encounters and has failed to secure the border during the Biden administration. The vice president toured border infrastructure, received briefings on drug interdiction, and was introduced by the mother of a fentanyl overdose victim. Immigration remains a leading voter concern in the battleground state of Arizona, where polls show greater support for Trump on the issue.

title: Trump escalates harsh rhetoric against immigrants, Harris
summary: Donald Trump delivered a speech in Prairie du Chien, Wisconsin, on Saturday that centered almost entirely on undocumented immigrants accused of violent crimes. He described such individuals as “monsters,” “stone-cold killers,” and “vile animals,” and displayed posters of people arrested for murder and other offenses alongside banners calling to “End Migrant Crime” and “Deport Illegals Now.” Trump blamed Vice President Kamala Harris and President Joe Biden for record migrant crossings, which government data show exceeded seven million during the current administration, and he repeated false claims that the 2020 election was fraudulent. He also referred to Harris as “mentally impaired” and “mentally disabled.” Harris’s spokesperson responded that Trump offered only “darkness.” The former president acknowledged the speech’s tone, stating, “This is a dark speech.” The remarks occurred days after Harris’s first campaign visit to the southern border, where she proposed tighter asylum rules and increased efforts to stop fentanyl trafficking. Studies have found no evidence that immigrants commit crimes at higher rates than native-born Americans. Several parents of victims of crimes or fentanyl overdoses spoke in support of Trump before the event.

title: Democratic mayors face withering attacks on ‘sanctuary city’ policies
summary: Four Democratic mayors from Boston, Chicago, Denver and New York testified for six hours before a Republican-led House committee that accused their sanctuary policies of shielding violent criminal immigrants. The mayors described the policies as efforts to aid recent migrant arrivals humanely while building trust with local immigrant communities and directing resources toward city priorities rather than federal immigration enforcement. They maintained that the measures had not increased crime. Committee Republicans repeatedly challenged the mayors with pointed questions, cited specific cases of offenses by undocumented immigrants, and suggested the officials could face prosecution or loss of federal funding. Democrats on the panel defended the local ordinances and disputed Republican characterizations of the cities as lawless. The hearing occurred as the Trump administration pursues mass deportations and has sued Chicago over its sanctuary law. New York Mayor Eric Adams faced additional scrutiny over his recent legal proceedings and reported cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

title: Bill nullifying D.C.’s ‘sanctuary city’ law advanced by House Republicans
summary:
A House committee advanced legislation Tuesday that would require the District of Columbia to cooperate with federal immigration enforcement by honoring detainer requests from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and sharing information on individuals in custody. The measure, introduced by Rep. Clay Higgins (R-La.), targets a 2019 D.C. law that limits such cooperation unless a judicial warrant is provided. It advanced along party lines and would need approval from the full House and Senate.

The bill includes an exception allowing D.C. to decline requests involving crime victims or witnesses. Proponents argued it balances enforcement needs with protections for those groups. Critics, including D.C. Delegate Eleanor Holmes Norton and immigrant rights advocates, contended that it undermines local policies and could discourage immigrants from engaging with law enforcement.

The action highlights ongoing congressional oversight of D.C. policies amid broader tensions over immigration and local governance. It comes as D.C. officials navigate relations with the Trump administration and Republican-led Congress on multiple fronts, including budget matters.

title: US Court says "metering" policy limiting asylum applications is illegal
summary: A divided panel of the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled on Wednesday that the federal government’s former metering policy at the U.S.-Mexico border violated immigration law. The policy, implemented in 2016 and expanded under the Trump administration, limited the number of asylum claims processed daily at ports of entry and turned away migrants once the cap was reached. In a 2-1 decision, the court held that federal law requires border officials to inspect all individuals who present themselves at designated crossings, regardless of whether they have physically entered the United States. The ruling affirmed a lower court’s finding that a 2019 asylum eligibility rule could not be applied to migrants previously turned away under metering, because they should have been permitted to apply when they first arrived. Judges Michelle Friedland and John Owens formed the majority, while Judge Ryan Nelson dissented. The Biden administration had argued that immigration statutes apply only after entry, but the court rejected that position. The case stems from a 2017 lawsuit filed by advocacy group Al Otro Lado and affected migrants. Metering was rescinded in 2021, though related restrictions remained in place during the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: How Biden's order restricting asylum claims actually works
summary: President Joe Biden announced a new policy on Tuesday halting asylum processing at the U.S.-Mexico border when daily illegal entries reach 2,500. The measure activates immediately, as current daily crossings average around 4,000. Under the policy, asylum claims will be suspended until daily arrests fall below 1,500 for seven consecutive days. Migrants denied asylum will receive deportation orders, facing potential criminal prosecution for subsequent attempts and multi-year bans on legal reentry. Unaccompanied minors remain exempt. The Biden administration states it is prepared for increased repatriations, though funding and diplomatic arrangements limit large-scale deportations to distant countries. Mexico has agreed to accept limited numbers of migrants from specific nations. Critics argue the policy endangers migrants and contravenes international protections, while legal challenges are anticipated. This represents the latest in a series of border measures by recent administrations aimed at deterring asylum seekers, following similar restrictions implemented in 2023.

title: Detention and that border "shutdown": What's really in Biden's bipartisan immigration deal
summary: The bipartisan border security legislation pairs roughly $20 billion in emergency spending with policy changes intended to restrict migration at the southern border. The measure would require the Department of Homeland Security to close most crossings once daily encounters average 5,000 migrants or reach 8,500 in one day, though unaccompanied minors from countries other than Mexico and Canada would be excluded from the count. It directs nearly $8 billion to Immigration and Customs Enforcement for expanded detention and nearly $7 billion to Customs and Border Protection for additional agents and overtime. Asylum processing would be accelerated through the hiring of more than 4,300 officers, with a goal of completing most cases within six months and stricter evidentiary requirements for applicants. The bill mandates continued use of prior appropriations for bollard-style border barriers and allocates $1.4 billion to assist state and local governments. It also creates up to 10,000 special immigrant visas for certain Afghan nationals, authorizes 250,000 new employment-based visas over five years, and includes funding to combat fentanyl trafficking. The legislation provides work authorization for some asylum applicants and limited relief for “Documented Dreamers,” but offers no new citizenship pathways for long-term undocumented residents. President Biden has described the package as necessary for orderly border management, while it faces resistance from both Republican leaders and progressive lawmakers.

title: Trump cuts exacerbate budget fights in red states
summary: Republican-led states are confronting significant budget challenges in 2026 due to provisions in President Donald Trump’s tax and spending legislation. The federal tax reductions and new mandates for Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program have resulted in added expenses and reduced revenues for several states, with some facing costs as high as $450 million annually. These developments have prompted legislatures to consider various spending reductions, including cuts to child care subsidies in Missouri, across-the-board agency reductions in Arizona, and decreases in disability services funding in Idaho. In Idaho, aligning state taxes with federal changes is projected to cost $155 million in 2026. Similar fiscal pressures have emerged in Iowa, where federal adjustments contributed nearly $350 million to an existing budget deficit exceeding $1 billion. While some states have chosen not to adopt all federal tax provisions to mitigate losses, others are implementing measures to comply with new program requirements. Officials in affected states have described the situation as requiring difficult trade-offs between maintaining services and managing reduced revenues.

title: Republicans lay groundwork for "total tax cliff" at end of Trump's term
summary:
Congressional Republicans are advancing legislation that would extend most provisions of the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act on a permanent basis while allowing several newer tax breaks to expire after 2028. The measures set to lapse include increases in the standard deduction and the deduction for seniors, an expanded child tax credit, and the elimination of taxes on tips, overtime pay, and car loan interest. House Freedom Caucus members and other fiscal conservatives have described the arrangement as creating a future “tax cliff” comparable to the one currently facing the 2017 cuts. 

In the Senate, members of the Finance Committee have indicated support for making core business provisions permanent but have expressed openness to reviewing or altering the additional worker- and family-oriented cuts. Some senators have voiced concern that temporary tax relief could simply defer difficult policy choices. The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office has estimated that the House-passed version would increase deficits by roughly $2.4 trillion over a decade, with additional interest costs raising the total to about $3 trillion. Democrats have argued that the bill disproportionately benefits higher-income taxpayers, while Republican leaders maintain that permanence for the 2017 framework remains the central objective.

title: Can Trump's tax cuts be made permanent? Tariffs, spending fights cloud the picture
summary:
Republican efforts to make permanent the expiring provisions of President Donald Trump’s 2017 tax cuts face significant obstacles in Congress. Lawmakers are divided over how to offset the cost of the cuts amid projections of continued high deficits and a national debt exceeding $36 trillion. House Republican hardliners have demanded at least $2 trillion in verifiable savings through spending reductions or a smaller tax package, while moderates have resisted proposed cuts to Medicaid. Some Republicans have suggested extending the 2017 provisions for another decade rather than making them permanent.

Party leaders maintain that the tax cuts will generate sufficient economic growth to cover much of their cost, projecting 2.6 percent annual GDP growth and $2.5 trillion in additional revenue over ten years. Independent analysts have described these forecasts as optimistic, noting that the 2017 cuts added roughly $1.9 trillion to the debt and that current proposals, including new exemptions for tips and overtime, could reach $6 trillion. They also cite risks from tariffs and tighter immigration policies that could constrain growth. Democrats have warned that the plan would increase deficits while reducing support for healthcare and other programs.

title: US Senate plan to make Trump tax cuts permanent raises "debt spiral" worry
summary: U.S. Senate Republicans are advancing a plan to make permanent the 2017 tax cuts enacted under President Donald Trump by using a parliamentary maneuver that bypasses Democratic opposition and omits projected revenue losses exceeding $4 trillion over ten years. The approach relies on the claim that tax policy would remain unchanged, allowing the measure to comply with Senate rules against expanding deficits beyond a decade. Several House Republicans, including Representatives Thomas Massie, Victoria Spartz, and David Schweikert, have opposed the strategy, describing it as fiscally irresponsible and an attempt to avoid spending reductions. The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office previously estimated that the original tax cuts increased the deficit by nearly $1.9 trillion over ten years, including economic effects. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget has warned that permanence could add up to $4.6 trillion in further deficits and raise the risk of a debt spiral through elevated interest costs, which already surpassed $1 trillion in the prior year. Senate Majority Leader John Thune has stated that debt projections are overstated. Republicans are revising a House-passed budget resolution to enable reconciliation procedures for enacting priorities, while also addressing expiring government funding after March 14 and the need to raise the debt limit.

title: US Senate Republicans pass measure to move forward on Trump's tax cuts
summary: The U.S. Senate approved a Republican budget blueprint in a 51-48 vote early Saturday, advancing a plan to extend President Donald Trump’s 2017 tax cuts and reduce federal spending. The measure enables budget reconciliation, permitting Republicans to pass related legislation on taxes, border security, and military funding without Democratic support or the 60-vote filibuster requirement. Senators Susan Collins and Rand Paul joined Democrats in opposition, and the bill now proceeds to the Republican-led House. Nonpartisan estimates project the agenda would add $5.7 trillion to the federal debt over the next decade, while Senate Republicans calculate the cost at $1.5 trillion and include a $5 trillion debt-ceiling increase. The blueprint seeks to offset some costs through spending reductions, prompting Democratic warnings about effects on Medicaid. During extended debate, Republicans added a reserve fund for Medicaid and Medicare but rejected multiple Democratic amendments on tariffs and social programs. The plan also envisions tighter border measures, expanded deportations, and increased military funding. The vote occurred against a backdrop of market declines following new trade tariffs.

title: Trump tax bill averts one debt crisis but makes future financial woes worse
summary: The bill passed by Congress extends the 2017 tax cuts, authorizes higher spending on border security and the military, and enacts reductions in Medicare and Medicaid. It also raises the federal debt ceiling by $5 trillion, eliminating the near-term risk of a U.S. default projected for late summer. Nonpartisan estimates project that the measure will add $3.4 trillion to the national debt over the next decade, reduce tax revenues by $4.5 trillion, cut federal spending by $1.2 trillion, and cause 10.9 million people to lose federal health insurance. Business tax provisions permitting full expensing of equipment and research costs are expected to support short-term economic growth. Analysts have noted that the added debt could increase Treasury supply and reduce foreign demand, potentially raising borrowing costs and contributing to inflation pressures. Bond market reaction has been muted, with investor focus remaining on corporate earnings and Federal Reserve policy. Treasury yields rose modestly on fiscal concerns, though some market participants viewed the legislation as secondary to other economic drivers.

title: What need to know about the child tax credit as both campaigns embrace it
summary:
Republican vice presidential candidate JD Vance proposed increasing the federal child tax credit to $5,000 per child for all families regardless of income. Vice President Kamala Harris called for restoring the expanded version used during the pandemic, including a $6,000 credit for families with newborns in the first year. Her running mate, Governor Tim Walz, signed a Minnesota law offering eligible families up to $1,750 per child on top of the federal amount.

The credit began in the late 1990s under President Clinton as a $500 nonrefundable benefit for middle- and upper-income families. It has since grown and changed with each administration, reaching a current maximum of $2,000 per child. A major temporary expansion in 2021 under the American Rescue Plan raised the maximum to $3,600, made the credit fully refundable, and allowed monthly payments. This change extended eligibility to 19 million children in low-income families and cut the child poverty rate in half before the provisions expired and poverty rates rose again.

Congress recently failed to enact a further expansion after opposition from some Republican senators. Analysts note the policy’s bipartisan history and its documented effects on household spending, food security, and child well-being, particularly for lower-income families.

title: Measuring the cost of extending Trump's tax cuts becomes a flashpoint in Congress
summary: Senate Republicans are pursuing a change in how the costs of extending President Donald Trump’s 2017 tax cuts are measured against future federal deficits. The Congressional Budget Office has estimated that making the cuts permanent would add nearly $4 trillion to deficits over the coming decade. Under the proposed approach, lawmakers would use a baseline that assumes the tax cuts remain in effect after their expiration, effectively treating their renewal as having no budgetary impact. Republicans plan to move forward without seeking a ruling from the Senate parliamentarian on whether the change complies with reconciliation procedures, which allow certain fiscal legislation to pass with a simple majority. Democrats have objected to the plan, describing it as a departure from Senate norms. Business groups have supported the effort, citing the need for long-term certainty in tax policy, while fiscal watchdog organizations have warned that it would reduce pressure to offset costs. House Republicans have instead assumed the extensions carry a cost and sought partial offsets through spending reductions. The outcome could influence both the size of the tax package and future congressional practices regarding deficit accounting.

title: How Trump's megabill transfers wealth in the US
summary: House Republicans passed a major tax and spending bill this week after lobbying by President Donald Trump. The measure extends 2017 individual income tax cuts and adds temporary provisions, including exemptions on tips and overtime pay. It reduces federal Medicaid spending by nearly $700 billion and Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program support by $267 billion over a decade, according to Congressional Budget Office estimates. The tax provisions are projected to increase the deficit by $3.8 trillion, while the overall package would add $3.1 trillion to the national debt including interest. Higher-income households would receive most tax relief, with the top 20 percent gaining the largest average cuts. Lower-income groups face net income losses from reduced benefits. The bill now moves to the Senate, where changes are expected before further House action. No major bipartisan discussions on long-term entitlement reforms are underway.

title: Investors see worsening US deficit outlook as tax bill heads to Senate
summary: Investors are concerned that a tax and spending bill moving through the Senate could raise projections for U.S. federal debt and keep bond yields elevated for longer. Moody’s downgrade of the U.S. sovereign credit rating on May 16 has added to market sensitivity about the debt trajectory. Long-dated bonds have come under particular pressure, with the 30-year yield reaching its highest level since October 2023 after a subdued response to a recent 20-year auction. The Congressional Budget Office estimates that the House-passed version of the bill would add roughly $3.8 trillion to the existing $36.2 trillion debt over the next decade. Analysts expect senators to seek changes that could shrink spending reductions and increase the overall cost. President Trump has set a target of July 4 for final passage. Administration officials have pointed to $1.6 trillion in spending cuts and projected revenue gains from tax reductions and tariffs, while some investors remain skeptical that the measures will sufficiently limit deficit growth. Market movements in yields may be monitored by lawmakers as the Senate debate proceeds.

title: GOP Lawmakers appear skeptical of Trump's $2,000 tariff rebate checks
summary: President Trump has proposed distributing $2,000 payments to low- and middle-income households using revenue from tariff increases. Republican lawmakers have shown limited support for the plan, with many preferring to apply the funds toward reducing federal deficits or financing health-policy measures related to the scheduled expiration of enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies. Members of Congress have cited the national debt as a primary concern and questioned the necessity of direct payments. Tariff revenue is projected to reach $158 billion in 2025 and $2.3 trillion over ten years, while the cost of the proposed checks is estimated between $280 billion and $607 billion. Some Republicans have also referenced risks of renewed inflation. Although administration officials have indicated that legislation would be needed and expressed confidence in securing passage, lawmakers report that detailed proposals have not been advanced. A small number of Republicans, including Sen. Josh Hawley, have endorsed tariff rebate checks, but broader congressional interest remains subdued.

title: Trump's "Big, Beautiful Bill" heads to senate, where new fights loom
summary: The House of Representatives passed a more than 1,000-page bill containing Republican tax and spending priorities early Thursday morning by a single vote following extended negotiations. The measure extends expiring tax cuts, incorporates provisions to eliminate taxes on tips, overtime pay, and Social Security benefits, and allocates additional funding for border security and the military. It also reduces federal spending on Medicaid, food assistance, and higher education. The legislation now advances to the Senate, where Republican leaders must reconcile differing priorities among their members. Some senators seek deeper spending reductions or permanent extensions of temporary tax cuts, while others have raised concerns about the higher state-and-local tax deduction cap and the rapid phaseout of clean-energy incentives. Any Senate amendments would require House approval before the bill could reach the president. The measure is estimated to increase federal deficits by $2.7 trillion through 2034. Republican leaders in both chambers have indicated a preference for limited changes to preserve the House agreement and meet a July 4 target.

title: Senate kills bipartisan tax bill
summary:
A bipartisan tax bill that passed the House earlier this year failed to advance in the Senate on Thursday after falling short of the 60 votes required for procedural approval. The measure, which received 48 votes in favor and 44 against, sought to restore expired business tax deductions for research and capital investments, expand the low-income housing tax credit, and enhance the child tax credit for lower-income families. It also aimed to terminate the employee-retention tax credit, a pandemic-era program that has exceeded original cost estimates due to fraud. 

Most Senate Republicans opposed the legislation, arguing it favored Democratic priorities and could be improved under different congressional control next year. A few Republicans, including Sens. Markwayne Mullin, Josh Hawley, and Rick Scott, supported it. On the Democratic side, Sens. Joe Manchin and Bernie Sanders voted against the bill, while Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer cast a procedural no vote to preserve the option for future consideration. 

Backers warned that the failure could lead to business layoffs and reduced support for disaster relief. The outcome highlights challenges in passing tax legislation under divided government, with larger expiring provisions from the 2017 tax law expected to shape future debates.

title: Republicans and democrats prepare for a tax-policy fight
summary: The US Labor Department reported that the economy added 272,000 jobs in May, exceeding economists' expectations, while average hourly wages rose and the unemployment rate increased to 4%. Major stock indexes closed lower, with the S&P 500 declining 0.1%, the Nasdaq Composite falling 0.2%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropping 0.2%. GameStop released first-quarter results in line with prior figures and announced plans to offer 75 million shares. Investor Keith Gill, known as "Roaring Kitty," stated during a livestream that he retains a large stake in the company; shares subsequently fell 40% and trading was halted multiple times. Provisions of the 2017 tax law affecting individuals are scheduled to expire at the end of 2025, setting up policy differences between Republicans favoring extensions and Democrats seeking income-based adjustments. A valuation dispute over Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago property was noted in connection with his civil fraud trial. Inflation has also increased costs for social activities such as dining out and entertainment.

title: House passes $78B tax bill in rare bipartisan vote
summary: The House passed a $78 billion bipartisan tax package Wednesday on a 357-70 vote, sending it to the Senate. The measure expands the Child Tax Credit to reach more families with multiple children and increases its refundable portion for low-income households, while also restoring several business tax provisions. It revives immediate deductions for research and development costs, provides relief for companies operating in the United States and Taiwan, boosts affordable housing tax credits, and expands disaster relief. Moderates from both parties supplied the two-thirds majority required under suspension of the rules. Some progressive Democrats opposed the bill, arguing it fell short of prior expansions that reduced child poverty, while conservative Republicans objected to provisions they described as welfare expansions, including payments to households with U.S.-born children of undocumented immigrants. The legislation now faces an uncertain path in the Senate, where Republican members have called for hearings and possible revisions, with action unlikely before March. Supporters noted the bill demonstrates Congress’s capacity to advance tax policy ahead of the 2025 expiration of major provisions from the 2017 tax law.
